the miso soup, which was just fine and warmed us up on a cold winter night. We followed with the edamame appetizer. Its hard to mess up edamame, and Ginza definitely didn't, but the dish could have used more seasoning to make an otherwise average dish stand out. There were other interesting appetizer choices, like seaweed salad, fresh spring rolls, and avocado salad, all of which are probably worth considering instead of the edamame. We then ordered the vegetable sushi roll, which contained avocado, asparagus, and cucumber (any of these could also be ordered individually within a roll). The roll consisted of six large pieces and was fresh and well made. There were four enticing vegetarian entrees on the menu; tofu vegetable teriyaki, tofu tempura, vegetable hibachi, and vegetable udon noodles. The udon noodles can be prepared pan-fried or in broth soup-style. The pan-fried udon noodles were quite bland, covered in a sauce that had little to no flavor or spice. The tofu teriyaki was slightly more interesting, with a thicker, more tasty sauce, but wasn't anything memorable and some of the vegetables were cold on the inside. The tofu was prepared crunchy out the outside but very wet and soft on the inside. Ginza does not put any hot sauce, pepper seeds, or chili paste on the table, and also do not offer a spiciness scale, so you can't really adjust what you get on your plate to accomodate for a lack of flavor. The lead-ins to the main course were not bad but not great, and the entrees were pretty lackluster. Overall, it seems as if Ginza doesn't have experience designing and preparing vegetarian items. Meat and fish eaters would likely have more success finding something satisfying. Price: The prices were very reasonable, as we ordered two soups, an appetizer, a sushi roll, and two entrees for under 30. We were hungry, so we didn't have enough left to bring home (although we may not have taken leftovers anyways due to lack of flavor), but the portion sizes are above average. Drinks: Ginza is BYOB but they do offer Japanese teas and sodas in addition to regular fountain drinks. Atmosphere: The restaurant is decorated very nicely with darkly painted walls and candlelit tables. There are tables for small and large parties, and enough space so that you aren't sitting directly on top of your neighbors. However, the restaurant is basically one big room and when the door opens on a cold night, you can feel the chilly air rush in if you are anywhere near the front. It isn't too difficult to find a parking spot on Liberty or one of its side streets. Service: We were seated immediately upon entering the restaurant and provided menus and glasses of water. Our waitress was very friendly and attentive, often checking our table and re-filling our water. We requested an addition of tofu to the udon noodles, which the waitress approved, but when the plate came the tofu was missing. We were also served our appetizer, sushi, and entrees within five minutes of each other, creating a table full of hot food getting cold.: cheap prices, large portions: average to below-average vegetarian food Would I go back again? Probably not, although I wouldn't stop a meat-eating friend from giving Ginza a shot.

the conclusion that flying with an airline should be a seamless experience between traveling on one of the world's busiest networks. In an effort to quantify some of the pain points I encountered with flying on different carriers I decided to create an algorithm (which I will not share with you, because you will only have to read this post).

This algorithm rates the different carriers over the factors that cause the most anxiety when traveling: delay and flight cancellation. I will explain the methodology and share the results in a series of posts.

## Methodology

I have broken the analysis into simple metrics:

1. **Cancellation Rate:** Number of cancelled flights divided by total number of flights that departed from a specific hub. A lower rate is better.

2. **Delay Rate:** Number of delayed flights divided by total number of flights departed. Total delay time is weighted higher by taking the square of the number of minutes delayed and dividing that total by the total number of flights. A lower rate is better.

Each metric is then rated

, where the buildings and landscape are designed to blend with the surrounding environment. A couple decades ago, they installed water fountains that play music to attract and welcome birds and wildlife. At certain times, the fountains turn off and a natural rock and grass filtration system cleans and recirculates the water to the next fountain, providing a continuous, clean water supply. It’s a beautifully simple solution to the constant maintenance that artificial ponds require.
I thought of the blog post while watching the different birds and squirrels interacting with the fountains. This photo shows a male cardinal that approached the fountain for a quick drink and then proceeded to bath in the spray from one of the other fountains. The squirrel to his left, I suspect, was trying to get his attention because the cardinal appeared to be getting distracted from his task.
It’s all about the environment, the natural order. The fountains provide a benefit for the local wildlife, while the local wildlife maintains the aesthetic and provides entertainment for humans.

, and I hope that I definitely wasn't. While growing up I noticed that people would throw these comments around a lot without thinking twice. It seems that they use it somewhat as an insult, implying that you don't have to work for what you have. However, the origin of this phrase doesn't derive from wealthy people at all. Instead it dates back to medieval Europe where poor children who would be born into wealth would be sometimes given special feeding cups with silver spoons to show off their status within their family. It was never meant as an insult, but a way to show off how wealthy you were in a period when illness was very common. Silver spoons where also used to show off how clean the spoon was, and thus a way to show off how wealthy you were since silver was a very expensive good. So when someone throws this around to anorexic person, they may see it as an insult but they are unknowingly doing the same thing as those rich medieval children with silver

expect delays, lost luggage, rude flight crew, empty middle seats, and boarding procedures that seem designed to maximize that airline's revenue, not make travelers happy. When you pay for something you want to know that you are getting what you paid for.
The problem with using air travel statistics as a basis for blaming specific airlines for these common traveler complaints or for overall safety is that these statistics are collected by the FAA for operational criteria, not consumer satisfaction. Statistics showing major US airlines consistently operating the safest percentage of flights are often used to deflect legitimate criticism of specific experiences with specific airlines. While overall safety may be comparable, consumers don't care about overall safety, so using safety as an argument to deflect legitimate complaints of poor service doesn't help anyone.
Legitimate consumer concerns are often about more than safety. Consumers want an airline that provides what it promises for the money paid. If an agent ensures you "direct flights" or "first-class" amenities, and then doesn't deliver, there should be consequences

Sunburst Shutters are a type of window treatment that combines the functionality of blinds with the style of shutters. They feature horizontal louvers, similar to blinds, but are mounted inside the window frame, just like traditional shutters. Sunburst Shutters are known for their modern and elegant appearance, offering a sleek and clean look for any room.
One of the key features of Sunburst Shutters is their ability to adjust the amount of light and privacy in a room. The horizontal louvers can be tilted to control the direction of light, allowing you to enjoy natural light while maintaining privacy. Additionally, the shutters can be fully opened or closed to block out light

Construction started in the 12th century, and it's been added to and altered over the centuries, reflecting Scotland's turbulent history. The most famous resident of the castle, apart from the various kings, queens and soldiers who have lived there, is the Stone of Destiny (or Stone of Scone). 1. Bread - Standard breads made with gluten-containing wheat are a primary concern. Always check labels for gluten-free options.

Or perhaps seen graffiti removed from a wall? This process is called sandblasting and it’s extremely effective at cleaning and etching a variety of surfaces. During sandblasting, high pressure air is pumped at a fine media, often sand. This sand is then blown at high speeds out the front of a nozzle, becoming a fine sandstorm that chips away at the surface of the object. Other materials can be used besides sand, ranging from non native to native materials. Abrasive materials are often used for etching and non abrasive materials like dry ice are used for colder jobs. The architecture is incredible, especially when you step back to the West Wing, where Washington made his farewell speech. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime place if you haven’t before, and it's even more rewarding if you've had some knowledge about the true history.
